reviews.text: [i] A deckbuilder where you create the dungeon you fight through? Sign me up! It’s creative, enjoyable, and offers enough content and depth to keep you busy for hours. [/i] [h1]📝 Main Pros, Cons, and Suggestions, followed by the Review:[/h1] 🟩 Pros: + Mid run saving is a massive QOL feature + A simple UI, with 3 coloured bars (health, energy, and light) + Various sized tiles featuring differing perks, rarities, and upgrades + The risk reward mechanic of losing health once your torch dims is well thought out + Building ruins to explore is creative, enjoyable, and thanks to building points, strategic as well + I personally love that there’s no minimap, its omission adds to the challenge and fun, as frustrating as it can sometimes be + 116 upgradable cards, 38 cantrips, 40 charms, 6 ruins, 12 weapons, 22 echoes, 62 creatures, and 3 characters (there’s A LOT to keep you busy) 🟥 Cons: - Boss fights (and combat in general) feels uninspiring - Some may not like the lack of minimap (I view it as an intentional design choice which complements the gameplay, rather than detracting from it) 🏷️ Suggestions: ~ Add a directional (or distance) indicator for the exit ~ More room variety, think destructible objects, gore (from defeated enemies), or torches on the wall to aid in navigation [h1] The Wardens Await [/h1] Build ruins, explore them, reach, defeat, and harvest The Warden, but be warned, time is against you. Once your torch fades, the darkness will begin to consume you. Into the Restless Ruins (RR) is as engaging as it is creative, serving as a refreshing take to the deck builder genre. Each turn you’re given a selection of cards, and with your limited build points, you build into the mist, unlocking rooms hidden in the shroud. The goal is to hunt the seals, claim them, weaken the Warden, and eventually, create a path to defeat them. Doing so won’t please them, however, prepare to fight against a horde of every increasing enemies, both in numbers and levels. Defeating enemies and feeding on their magical energies earns favours which can be exchanged for additional cards, adding both complexity and rewards to your ruins. Outside of the building and combat, you’ll also need to juggle your health and torch, both crucial for survival. Health is self-explanatory, but your torch, well that slowly dims – If it dims enough, not only can’t you see far, you begin losing health rapidly. Finally, each night your skull bar will fill. Once reaching a skull, a curse will be added to your hand. Let the bar fill fully and you will fail – A simple system which does a good job at keeping you on your toes. Overall, Into the Restless Ruins is a unique addition to the deck builder genre. While I don’t enjoy the combat, the building aspect is a treat, feeling like a game of Tetris at points. It’s a solid buy, both for fans and newcomers to the genre! This game gives you the satisfaction of planning and building a dungeon that lets you get to your goals and stack buffs perfectly. Then you run out of light, panic and suddenly its an inescapable labyrinth in which you have no idea what the right way is. 10/10, I will be playing this one for a lot.

[quote] [h1]比爬塔更有趣！这款游戏让你用卡牌"盖房子"打怪[/h1] 在遍地都是"爬塔like"的卡牌游戏市场，《勇闯无尽遗迹》拿出了挺有意思的解法：把卡牌构筑玩成了"地牢施工队"。玩家手里的每张卡牌不再是对战招式，而是直接化作迷宫里的房间与走廊——这手"卡牌即地牢"的设计，让传统DBG（牌库构筑，Deck-Building Game）的套路瞬间有了新滋味。 本作最吸引我的地方莫过于"战略施工"的乐趣，游戏卡牌种类繁多，不仅稀有程度（稀有度越高给的Buff收益也会很不错）、结构不同，出口个数和出口位置分布也会不同。比如天文台和枯萎林地虽然都只需要占用一个地块，但是天文台给的buff是随机清除一个房间的迷雾（迷雾效果后面会讲到），出口数量有两个分布在左右，而枯萎林地效果则是恢复血量，出口数量有三个，并且后续还有同类卡牌的plus版本，出口数量、结构布局也会有不同。每次在牌桌上纠结的不是出牌顺序，而是如何把不同功能的房间拼成高效迷宫。这种既像搭积木又像解谜的体验，配合肉鸽的随机性，玩起来确实上头。 https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3479628860 当然你并不是肆无忌惮的随意释放所有手牌，每回合都会有建造点数来限制你能打出的卡牌，建造点数是可以通过特殊手段提升，比如在收割模式中找到铁匠铺让下回合能够使用的建造点数更多。地图上有很多被迷雾遮挡住的地块，我们主要找的就是封印地块（解除封印地块会迎来怪物潮，并且还会给你福利卡）， https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3479628820 因为要去打最后的Boss必须要破除所有的封印地块才能到达。多块迷雾之中只有一块是封印地块，其他地块可能只是经验、游戏内货币、武器池以及随机事件等。 https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3479628802 当每局建造点数耗尽，就是玩家下本之时，下本的战斗是自动的，有一种玩吸血鬼幸存者的感觉，击败敌人会获得经验，经验满了就能升级获取新的建筑卡。除了自身血量还要关注火把亮度，火把耗尽就会陷入黑暗， 持续扣除血量，虽然本作死亡并不会导致游戏失败，但是死亡次数多了也不好，死亡会涨恐惧值，达到不同阶段的恐惧值会给你DeBuff卡，当恐惧值满了也就意味着本局游戏结束。一定要合理把控并放置能够给火把“续命”、减缓火把消耗的地块，比如营火可以补充火把、烽火可以减缓火把消耗速度。不过下本没有小地图，全靠玩家记忆力过自己的迷宫，看着自己精心设计的"迷宫陷阱"困住的不是魔物，而是自己差点没绷住，上了物理外挂，下本先截图置顶地图了，笑哭.jpg。 游戏内事件地块也挺多的，但是事件地块收益不大，要不是每次都猜错封印地块，我可能不太愿意去这些事件地块。贤鸡可以用游戏币升级卡牌，商人狼人沃尔弗可以购买饰品卡牌，武器地块还是值得去的，解锁一次就能在后面建筑获取重复使用。 作为肉鸽老饕，个人最欣赏本作的"动态难度"设计。每次重开不仅能遇到关卡中的未知敌人，连迷宫生成规则都会变化。上次靠传送门速通的套路，下次可能因为没Roll到营火地块而火把耗尽暴毙。这种永远猜不透的对局，再加上每次结束根据对局完成的任务解锁的卡包，让本作的重复耐玩度提升不少。不过初期卡池较浅时，构筑组合有限，需要多肝几局才能体验完整策略深度。 总的来说，本作将DBG与地牢建造缝合的作品，既保留了卡牌构筑的策略深度，又用空间解谜元素带来新鲜感。如果你厌倦了传统爬塔模式，想体验新奇的肉鸽世界，不妨试试这场另类的"迷宫施工大赛"。毕竟，能亲眼看着自己的牌组从平面卡牌变成立体迷宫，这体验本身就已经值回票价。 [quote] 游玩百态，将游玩心得用汉语化作玩家的指明灯，(๑•̀ㅂ•́)و✧ [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35402408/]点击这里关注汉化语录~[/url] 如果喜欢这个评测，请点个赞让更多人看见 [/quote] [/quote]
Welcome to my dungeon. It's just 30 armories stacked in a straight line.

Love the idea of the game, the dungeon building aspect of it is cool, done by a few games before, but it's a mechanic I've always liked, and is implemented well here. The addition of the light mechanic, having a limited time to navigate the ruins adds a nice little twist too, so I appreciate that. And the pixel art, 8-bit music, with the nods to Scottish history, all create a nice atmosphere overall. However, the combat side of things is where the game is a let down. There just isn't much going on with the weapons or the enemies, and it feels wholly unsatisfying. Even the bosses don't really have much to them, never feeling at risk in the encounters, and the whole game ultimately feels kind of easy if you play even a little cautiously. This game could have been great with a decent combat system, but without it gets boring a little too quickly, and that combined with a lack of difficulty ultimately means I can't recommend it.
The second map is just too large this early on. Especially with a deadly boss at the end.

Get's extremely repetitive and boring very quickly... The concept is very cool, but the drafting/deckbuilding isnt interesting enough and the exploring of your dungeons isnt interesting enough either; it sadly results in two very mediocre games put together

I very rarely leave negative reviews, and I didn't hate this game. But dear god did it frustrate me immensely with its mix of brilliant and awful design decisions. Okay first off: combat. It is bad and uncompelling. It's just not engaging. It lacks any particular strategy. There's mild positioning that happens. The combat progression is slowly and largely irrelevant. Maybe I'll come back w/ a review that's like "actually combat really opens up after the 20th hour" but somehow I doubt it. Then the leveling. I have very mixed feelings on this. Building out your deck is fun. Adding new cards to a deck is fun. But there's very little point in adding 5 copies of bonfire to your deck when you could just skip almost every ward and keep your deck leaner. Yes, there are a couple archetypes that make that less good, but generally speaking most of the "reward" that you get from killing mobs is booster chaff that you end up throwing away. Oh but the actual building? The room placement? Glorious. Incredibly fun. And then the mad scramble to get back to your portal as your torchlight fades and your vision goes black while you're somehow managing to get lost in a labyrinth of your own design that you tetrised together so you could get all the bonuses? The death by hubris is incredibly humbling. And it's rewarding to work past it. And that's not to talk about the weird building archetypes and progression and pseudo-heat system that I don't.....love but.....don't hate either? I feel very similarly to this as I did to Cult of the Lamb: extremely compelling management sim with extremely mid combat, where you're going to spend most of your time in combat unfortunately.

I see the vision, and it's definitely an interesting one, but the execution is tedious and not very fun. The key part of the game here is building the map. The map will be sectioned off by seals. You can only access the next part of the map by finding a seal and unlocking it. There will be rooms on the map hidden by fog. You have to figure out which one of these rooms is the seal by using your cards to build rooms and explore those obscured rooms. As you open seals, more and more rooms become hidden by fog, so you end up having to do a lot of tetris and exploring to figure out where all the seals are. Once you unlock the last seal, you are free to fight the boss. The gameplay loop consists of placing rooms from your hand like a typical deckbuilder. You draw 5 cards and spend energy to place them. Once you are done, you raid the dungeon you have built. Once you are done raiding, you must run all the way back to an escape portal and start anew. Essentially placing rooms, raid, escape. Not all rooms are just boring hallways. Some will give you permanent stats for placing them, others might buff you for the current or next room, or give you resources. As you raid, you have to manage your health and torchlight. The torch is constantly draining, so you can place rooms that allow you to fill it back up. Spacing these out properly is key. While you raid, there are enemies. Combat is done very similar to Vampire Survivors, except way more dull. You can only have two weapons at a time, and the only ones I've found have not been very interesting. Combat is a complete afterthought as there isn't much to it. No dodging, aiming, or anything interactive besides moving around. And this is where the game becomes quite dull. Exploring your dungeon becomes tedious as it gets larger and larger. You have to memorize your map, which is part of the challenge. You can't look at the map after you enter, so you have to remember how you built it, which gets progressively more difficult as your dungeon becomes more labyrinthine. As you kill enemies, you gain XP very similar to Vampire Survivors, but leveling up only offers you three new cards. You will be skipping the majority of these because you don't want your deck to be too big and that's literally the only point of leveling up. Overall...I see the vision. The map making part and then trying to survive to explore it, all while building up permanent stats so you can take on the boss is a neat concept. The actual raiding the dungeon part, which takes up a HUGE amount of your game time, is too dull for me to continue playing. As a result, I will be refunding this one.

The dungeon-building aspect of this game is really cool. The art and music are very good. The combat is where it falls apart. You can discover new weapons during a run, but the weapons you pick up are not necessarily an upgrade from the default starting weapon. The axe and the dagger both felt like a huge downgrade from the sword. I felt like the game was punishing me for picking them up. There is no meta-progression for combat skills or stats. I know the devs have said combat isn't the focus of the game, but its an auto-battler. Combat is an integral mechanic. And it just doesn't feel good. You can't choose your starting weapon, you can only swap weapons during a run by building and then visiting a specific room. This really doesn't make sense to me because enemy difficulty scales as you go into the later dungeon zones, but your combat ability does not. This game is pretty fun for 2-3 hours. But it gets more and more frustrating and tedious as you progress. I would recommend it if the combat system was reworked to include some meta-progression so you felt like your character's stats were scaling alongside the enemies.

This was either going to be a very positive negative review, or a very negative positive review, and it's close. I've chosen the negative, ultimately because I will be refunding this game. Building your own path forward is truly novel, and I suspect that between the decisions you're forced to make and their consequences that you're forced to confront, a portion of that sense of freshness will persist for a long time despite this game's pitfalls. You have an obligation to yourself to make the dungeon traversable, and there's plenty of obstacles to that. Some exist in the world- the myriad side rooms that you must investigate (and branch off to) to find seals and weapons, the rocks and rubble interrupting a potential straight path, and the sheer vastness of most caves all already mean you will be building a sprawling dungeon. More clever are the obstacles that come in the rooms you're given, as the rooms with more potent effects (such as armories, workshops, forges and training rooms) come in awkward shapes that not only make it more difficult to build towards a destination but also cause the path to curve, split and ultimately complicate navigation through the dungeon, with too many of them creating a maze you never intended. This all is genius, and beautifully crafted. I have one major hitch with the game, and where other negative reviews will cite the simplistic combat, I consider that another of the game's strengths- it's designed to take up your limited time in the dungeon in a way that incentivizes adding those complicated rooms mentioned earlier. I think that's a good choice. Where this game fails is that you don't have to put any work into gathering tools to build your dungeon, as the very best pieces are in your deck at all times. Venturing into the dungeon and slaying enemies will reward you with new cards (dungeon pieces), which you can add to your deck to gain more variety in what you place. That is, these cards are -supposed- to act as a reward. But these cards are never consumed. Once you go through your deck, it gets reshuffled and dealt to you fresh, with every card intact. In other words, you're never at risk of running out of components, so every rare addition or niche shape you work for only serves to pollute your deck. And this is felt doubly so, because while some of these additions can be helpful, the essentials that you start with are genuinely what you want to use the most. These are rooms which you can visit for healing, power ups & extra exploration time (which, if you run out of during an exploration, drains your health at a nearly unsalvageable rate.) Nearly all of them come in straightforward shapes that can be nestled anywhere, without mandatory twists or branches but with doors that allow for it if you so desire. And most of all, these rooms give you powerful passive boosts just for being placed in the dungeon. These are provided to you in the deck you start with, and since used cards just reshuffle themselves back together, you have infinite copies of them from the start. Which means you already have the most powerful deck built from the start. In what is, supposedly, a deckbuilder. You will inevitably add a small number of cards to your deck, but any more than that is foolhardy, and risks giving you a hand full of awkward junk that couldn't build a path across a street. There's nothing to actively work for. I think if perhaps only corridors re-shuffled whereas room cards could only be placed once, and you had to earn every extra copy of those essential rooms, the game would hold my interest. But as is, the game is missing a critical aspect of its own gameplay, and is fairly incapable of presenting risks to weigh. It treats these extra cards as boons, and unlocks more options for extra cards as you progress with the game to evoke a sense of increasing possibilities, and of getting stronger. And I think that reflects on it as a game that just doesn't understand itself well enough.

I didn't realize I'd beat the game in one day. I feel a little frustrated that the game doesn't have more content for the price. The maze/dungeon building part of the game was fun, but the combat was boring because weapon choice doesn't seem to matter much and training rooms (power ups) feel very weak. Overall, the concept is great but the game is much easier than I thought it'd be and is over in a blink.

Into the Restless Ruins, developed by Ant Workshop Ltd and published by Wales Interactive, offers a fresh and inventive take on the roguelike deckbuilder genre by blending dungeon construction with card-based strategy. Released in 2025, the game distinguishes itself through its unique mechanic that allows players to shape the dungeon layout itself using a deck of cards, rather than simply battling through a pre-designed environment. This innovative design creates a compelling mix of strategic planning and procedural generation that keeps each playthrough feeling new and rewarding. The gameplay revolves around nightly excursions into mysterious ruins, where players expand the dungeon by placing cards that represent rooms, corridors, and other elements. Each card added not only changes the dungeon’s architecture but can also trigger synergies and bonuses that affect the player’s combat efficiency and progression. This system demands a thoughtful balance between building a cohesive layout and optimizing for the strongest combinations of cards and relics. Rather than controlling the hero directly in combat, players rely on an auto-battle system that rewards well-planned dungeon design and deck composition, adding a unique layer of indirect tactical control. Deeply rooted in Scottish folklore, the game’s narrative and world-building add considerable depth and charm. Players encounter various mythological creatures and characters, such as the Hen Wife and the Wulver, who provide meaningful interactions and gameplay benefits. These elements enrich the atmosphere, making the journey through the ruins feel like a true folklore-inspired adventure. The ultimate goal is to gather Glimour, a mystical resource from the cursed denizens of the ruins, and confront The Warden—a formidable boss drawn from legend—in hopes of unlocking the Maiden’s promise. This storytelling framework provides motivation and context that elevates the roguelike experience beyond simple dungeon crawling. The scope and variety of Into the Restless Ruins are impressive. With over a hundred cards across multiple categories, dozens of unique enemies, including several bosses, and an assortment of passive charms and weapons to unlock, the game offers plenty of content and strategic options. Each run can feel dramatically different depending on the cards drawn and the dungeon layout chosen, encouraging players to experiment with different strategies and builds. The meta-progression system adds further depth, rewarding players with new relics and cards that can shift how future runs play out, maintaining long-term engagement and replayability. While the game’s innovative mechanics and thematic richness have been widely praised, there are some points of contention among players. Some have noted occasional technical issues such as performance dips and crashes, which can disrupt the flow of gameplay. Others have expressed a desire for more variety in enemy behavior and dungeon design to deepen the combat challenge and keep encounters feeling fresh. These critiques point toward areas where the game could be polished further, and it appears the developers are attentive to community feedback with plans for future updates and improvements. Overall, Into the Restless Ruins stands out as a thoughtfully crafted and original roguelike deckbuilder that successfully combines strategic dungeon building with an evocative narrative inspired by Scottish folklore. Its unique gameplay loop, combining card placement with indirect combat management, offers a refreshing experience for genre enthusiasts. Though not without its flaws, the game’s strong foundation, rich thematic world, and abundant content make it a rewarding title for players seeking a challenging and atmospheric roguelike adventure. As the game continues to evolve, it holds significant promise to become a memorable and enduring entry in the deckbuilder and roguelike communities. Rating: 8/10

This is a really fun game and unique game. There aren't many games that let you build the level as you explore them. It certainly has some bullet heaven elements, but don't think that its like Vampire Survivors where you can carry and upgrade multiple weapons that are automatically firing all at once. You can only carry two weapons at a time, one melee and one projectile weapon. You're also being timed so you have hurry. The beneficial cantrips are really helpful, so use them, but you may want to counter them by using something that will make it harder because lowing the dread lowers how quickly you level up. The graphics are pretty minimal, but still colorful. I would still like the characters to be a bit more detailed through, and I would love for there to be a bit more lore involving all of the different monsters. I wish there were some more games like this. I love first person shooters, and I wish there was a first person shooter rogue like or rogue lite where you'd build the levels as you explore them. That could be really fun, especially if it had multiple well designed weapons and enemies.

This one is a short playthrough but an awesome one: it was my favorite game of 2025, and it's a criminal shame that so few people have heard of it. As a big fan of roguelike deckbuilders, roguelike ARPGs, and the classic tabletop game Castles of Mad King Ludwig, this game felt perfectly tailored to me. Think of it as an experience in which Phase I starts with you playing CoMKL, then you play low-fi Hades during Phase II (on the map that you made in Phase I), then you strategize about where on the worldmap to expand your dungeon next. A really satisfying strategy loop, just enough RNG to keep you permanently on your toes and excited for the next run, and a totaly cromulent action layer that gets its best mileage out of the fact that there is no minimap...you are forced to remember the dungeon you just laid out. Diabolical and awesome. Seriously, just pick this one up, you'll thank me.

This is a neat little game that incorporates Scottish folklore as you create your own dungeon. There's lots of replayability here, with your character leveling up as you play through scenarios, unlock new cards and cantrips, and interact with characters during your run. I didn't expect to enjoy this game as much as I did, as I primarily bought this game to support developers who are willing to put in the extra effort to include minority languages like Scottish Gaelic and Welsh. I would definitely recommend this game for anyone who wants to try a new take on roguelike deckbuilders. Chòrd e rium gu mòr - tha e glè spòrsail! :)

A fun roguelike that is a mix of deck builder and dungeon crawler. You have a deck of cards that represent dungeon rooms and when you start a run, you will build a basic three room entry dungeon, then once you run out of build points you will enter your new little dungeon and explore it for loot and fight some monsters. The longer you can stay in there and earn XP the better as every time you level you will add a new room for your deck. The idea is to last as long as possible then escape using the entrance portal. Once you have escaped, you can use your new rooms to build more of the dungeon. As the game goes by, the game adds little curse skulls, one after each run, more if you die, when the skull curse bar reaches a certain point you will get a curse which will make your runs harder in some way. So you are encouraged to try and escape rather than die in the dungeon. As you slowly build more you will finally access the rooms dotted around the map that are covered in mist. Once you make a path to those rooms you can go there to uncover them and see whats in there. It might be an NPC, a room with a bit of loot, or if you are lucky a Seal room. In the Seal rooms you activate the seal and fight a wave of monsters. Opening a seal opens up blocked off areas of the dungeon making more room for you to build. Unlocking seals will also lower your curse bar a bit, keeping those nasty curses off your back a bit. It also should be noted that if the curse bar ever completely fills to the end, you are consumed by darkness and lose the game. Unlock enough seals and you will eventually make your way to the dungeon boss and if you can beat them you have finished that particular dungeon and will unlock the next. Each dungeon location has a slightly different theme and ways the seals unlock as well as a different boss. Its quite an interesting take on the whole genre mixing together card building, dungeon construction and dungeon crawling. Its quite interesting and there are a bunch of cards to unlock and the cards can also be upgraded. The base rooms you start with are corridors, rooms to recharge your torch and health etc, but as you go along you will unlock training rooms, forges, stables, graveyards etc, all with their own little kinks and twists on gameplay. Its a solid little title and I like it quite a bit. The asking price is very reasonable to given how long you are likely to get out of it. Im about 6 hours in so far and have done 3 of the dungeons and beaten their bosses. A word of advice: Plan your dungeon well as you construct it. Remember you have to walk through it yourself. If you make it a maze, you are making a maze for yourself to get lost in. Spread out your healing and torch recharge places logically so you always have SOMEWHERE nearby(ish) that you can get to to recharge if things get desperate. And dont think the signpost rooms are useless, you can move the direction of the sign yourself, I always havint the signs point to the way to go to reach the exit portal. Can be super useful when you are running for exit low and health and torchlight. Anyway, well worth it!

[i]---See where this game landed on my Rogue-like/lite Deckbuilder Tier List beneath this rec!---[/i] This has the deckbuilding room mechanic that was also used by [b]Blue Prince[/b] which released around the same time. I much prefer this game to that one, as it’s far more gamey. [b]Into the Restless Ruins[/b] reminds me quite a lot of [b]Dungeon of the Endless[/b]. That game was a bit harder and slightly more complex to grasp, and has very different mechanics, but the result of everything both games do ends up being quite similar. Both games have a planning phase where you’re deciding which way to branch out followed by a phase where you fight and explore. This one doesn't really have meta progression, just unlocks which don't necessarily make you stronger, so the roguelite tag that players have given this is misleading. Combat is pretty basic, you autoattack in the direction you’re facing like in many bullet heaven games. It’s quite easy to accidentally take damage by misjudging your distance from enemies while trying to keep close and in attacking range of them. I think the hitboxes could be tighter, but it wasn’t enough of a gripe to stop me having fun with it. Your character has a few basic stats like attack speed, attack size, crit chance. You can acquire some different weapons. This aspect of the game is pretty minimalistic and you don’t get to create very different combat builds. Unlocking more cards can be disadvantageous because it pollutes the card pool, making it harder to draw the cards that you find to be most useful. Most games get around this by letting you ban x number of cards from appearing in runs but there is no such remedy here. I find that in most cases, it's best to ignore most of your card reward choices so you can cycle through a small group of good cards but the game doesn't appear fully aware of itself when it comes to this. I feel like this aspect of the game could have used more thought by the developers. The music is pretty cool synthwave - I was vibing to it. I beat all of the levels within the first 8-10 hours and I think I only failed a level once. That said, I thought many of my victories were lost causes, but somehow managed to still win. Beating the hard versions of the levels adds some longevity to the game, however there is no achievement for doing it. There is one hard one to shoot for though, which involves beating a level with maximum dread multiplier which, as of now, only 0.2% of players have achieved. Going for all of the other achievements can greatly expand the time you get out of the game though (I did them all). This is a fun game and an easy recommendation, I'm surprised it isn't more well-known. The retro graphics style is possibly a factor in that, but I personally like this style. So far having a half dozen maybe hours, it's alright. I like the overall gameplay concept of placing the tiles to make your dungeon rooms you then traverse... In terms of moment to moment gameplay though for a roguelike, it can't really touch something like Megabonk for instance or something similar in moment-to-moment interest/gameplay. Earning the various tiles through the leveling, feels a bit slow. And some of the cantrips you choose before runs don't seem seem to align with what you think they'll be doing, based on the description. The one that says your torch starts the run empty for instance, does not also say it burns down in like 5 seconds, despite filling it at campfires. So, some tiles/or cards do not have adequate or even accurate descriptions. That's not to touch on the music, which although is fine enough, it's very repetitive. aside from these complaints, I like the game overall, it's just not all it could be for the concept, I'd like to see run with in a future game by someone. I wouldn't buy at full price, but in a bundle for cheap it may be an okay buy as something to play.

Surprised that the top reviews for this are so negative; have had a lot of fun with this, a really well designed mashup of genres that when you average out enjoyment by price is a steal. Closest comparison I can think of is Blue Prince mixed with Vampire Survivors but it has its own vibe and feel that is pretty unique. Complaining about the combat seems to miss the point of the game; its closer to a speed run that you build yourself than a dungeon crawler or action RPG. Likewise the issues surrounding lack of difficulty seem a little overblown, while the game balance is not perfect it has an light arcadey feel where the point is not about whether you will win but how well you will win (this may change, I haven't cleared all the dungeons yet) Great to pick up and play and dive into every now and again. If you think there's a chance you will like this then you should definitely pick it up its the definition of a hidden gem.
